job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Emeka Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mornings are lectures or the library in Manchester, I'm doing a master's in marketing analytics. Evenings, three or four nights a week, I deliver food on an e-bike for about 25 pounds an hour on a good night, less on a bad one. I get home around midnight and then apply for jobs, which feels like shouting into a well.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the story behind getting here?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did a marketing degree at Salford and passed, no first, no internship, because every summer I worked in a warehouse. My dad drives a taxi and my mum works nights at a care home, so there's love but no money to spare. I owe about 38,000. I picked analytics because the job ads for plain marketing all asked for a year of experience, and analytics at least sounded like something with a future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it on your course, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, maybe the hype dies and the market steadies. But I'd also say to my mates that it won't fix anything, because the problem was never the technology. It's that firms don't want to train anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd stay where I am, which isn't great. Plateau just means the same rough deal, five marketing jobs in Manchester and 400 of us applying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the course in September and send about 15 applications a week, tailored, not copy and paste. I'd keep the delivery nights and use the AI chatbot like I do now, for tidying data and first drafts. And I'd ask my tutor to introduce me to a couple of local agencies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit stuck, like running on a treadmill. I'm not scared, just tired of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the delivery work pays the rent. What happens if the app cuts your shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd be in trouble. Rent in my shared flat is 450 a month and my dad can't help, so I'd ask the app for more shifts and eat at my parents' on Sundays. I've got maybe three weeks of money if everything stops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where do you place the blame for how hard it is to get a first job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Employers, mostly, and a government that lets them. They want a ready-made worker with two years of experience, and none of them will pay for the two years. A rule that firms must offer paid graduate placements would fix a lot.

say: I'd tell mates it won't fix anything, because firms never wanted to **train** anyone.
I'd say it's fine if the market steadies.
think: I'm in the same rough deal: about **five** suitable local jobs and 400 applicants.
do: Send about **15 tailored applications** a week from September.
Keep the delivery nights and use a chatbot for tidying data.
Ask my tutor to introduce me to local **agencies**.
feel: **Stuck**, like on a treadmill, more tired than afraid.
S0.quote: Plateau just means the same rough deal, five marketing jobs in Manchester and 400 of us applying.
fieldNote: Blames **employers** who refuse to train, and wants paid graduate placements as a rule.
Steady with AI: already uses a chatbot for data and drafts.
**Three weeks** of money keeps even a quiet world stressful.

steps.text: Send 15 tailored applications a week from September
Keep the evening delivery shifts on the e-bike
Eat Sunday dinners at my parents' to save money

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it on your course, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's already happening and we should get a say. Unions for delivery riders and for office workers should ask for training time paid by the company, not by us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'm on the wrong side of the line. Writing copy, reports, campaign summaries, that's the junior stuff and a chatbot does it in seconds. The people with experience stay, the new ones don't get hired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lean into the analytics part, learn the tools agencies pay for, and build a small portfolio of three real projects on my laptop. I'd do a free evening course on a dashboard tool, and keep delivering. And I'd join the riders' group properly, not just turn up for the beers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but a bit excited too. It's different when you can see a skill you could actually learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of a marketing job do you think AI takes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing, scheduling posts, reporting numbers back to a client. A person who can explain what the numbers mean to a worried boss still has a job, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use a chatbot now and then. Would you use it more in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but only once it's proven, I'm not an early adopter. I'd use it for the first draft and then check it carefully, because a client will blame me, not the tool.

say: I'd say unions should demand **paid training time** from the company.
I'd tell people it's already happening in the junior jobs around us.
think: Junior **copywriting and reporting** jobs are the first to go and I have no experience.
Being able to explain numbers to a client may save me.
do: Build a **portfolio** of three real analytics projects.
Take a free evening course on a dashboard tool.
Join the **riders' group** properly and keep delivering.
feel: **Anxious** but a bit excited about a skill I can learn.
S1.quote: A person who can explain what the numbers mean to a worried boss still has a job, I think.
fieldNote: Moves from complaint to a concrete plan: **portfolio** and tools.
Steady adopter: will use AI once proven and checks the output.
Union thinking is practical, asking for **paid training time**.

steps.text: Build three real analytics projects for a portfolio
Finish a free evening course on a dashboard tool
Join the delivery riders' group and go to meetings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it on your course, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly the moment unions and governments are for. Pay people, protect them, slow down the firing. I'd be loud about it online and at the riders' group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think a degree in marketing is dead on arrival. Every job I trained for is thinking work, and I'd be a 26-year-old with 38,000 of debt and a delivery bike. The bike jobs have about three more years, then robots come for that too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop applying for marketing jobs and look hard at anything hands-on or in the care sector, like my mum's workplace. I'd keep delivering as long as it lasts. And I'd go back to my parents' spare room to save the 450 rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. That's the right word. I'd lie awake doing sums on the debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your dad that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my dad, who's driven a taxi for 30 years, that his job is also on the list. We'd sit at the kitchen table and I'd say none of us did anything wrong, and that we'd pool whatever we have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from the government in those two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A basic income, free retraining, and a tax on the companies that gain. If that doesn't happen in two years there will be riots, and I'd be in the street with the riders.

say: I'd say governments must **pay and protect** people, and slow the firing.
I'd be loud about it online and at the riders' group.
think: A marketing degree could be **dead on arrival** with 38,000 of debt.
Even delivery work only has about three more years.
do: Stop applying for marketing and look at **care sector** jobs.
Move back into my parents' **spare room** to save 450 a month.
feel: **Alarmed**, lying awake doing sums on the debt.
S2.quote: I'd tell my dad, who's driven a taxi for 30 years, that his job is also on the list.
fieldNote: Family framing: wants his **father** and himself to pool what they have.
Turns political fast: basic income, retraining, **tax** on winners.
Plans to switch fields to hands-on care work for the extra three years.

steps.text: Apply for care assistant jobs near my mum's workplace
Move back into my parents' spare room
Ask my family to pool money for bills
Vote and march for basic income and free retraining

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it on your course, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to make a plan but not enough to be relaxed. We need training funds set up now, not in 2031 when it's too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be worried, but I'd also see a gap I could use. With five years I could get a first job, pay a chunk of the debt, and learn how these systems work from the inside. I'd be 29 when it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any analytics job in the next year, even a poor one, and spend 5 hours a week on the tools. I'd send 300 a month to the loan. And I'd keep my place in the riders' group because collective voice matters more later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but steady. It's a fair fight if I start now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years let you do that two would not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It lets me get a first real pay slip, which changes everything. A payslip means a mortgage chance, a rental reference, a proper start. Two years wouldn't have given me that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do first if the year was 2027 and you could see it coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay down the loan hard and ask my mum about the care assistant route, which is a safe backup. I'd also start saving a small amount in a boring account, 100 a month.

say: I'd say five years is enough for a **plan** but not for relaxing.
I'd push for training funds now, not in 2031.
think: I could get a first job and learn the systems from **inside**.
I'd be 29 when it lands, with less debt.
do: Take any **analytics job** in the next year, even a poor one.
Send **300 a month** to the loan.
Keep my place in the riders' group.
feel: **Anxious** but steady, because it's a fair fight if I start now.
S3.quote: With five years I could get a first job, pay a chunk of the debt, and learn how these systems work from the inside.
fieldNote: Time converts fear into a **timeline**: job, debt, skills, in that order.

steps.text: Take the first analytics job offered, even a poor one

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it on your course, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the best-case version, and we should use the decade to build things properly, like retraining and a shorter working week. People should push now, while there's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm a lot more relaxed. By 34 I could have a career, a flat and a changed job. I'd just worry that the gains go to the owners and not people like my mum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a first job, build my skills, and aim for a role that's about talking to clients and explaining. I'd pay the loan down steadily and save a deposit. I'd also try to be one of the people who teach others the tools, since I'm good at that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. It's almost normal worry, about rent and loans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does ten years change what you tell younger people?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell younger students to learn something that makes them useful to a person, not a spreadsheet, and to do a placement even if unpaid for a month. And not to put it all on one degree like I did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you still worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the rewards go to a few and the rest of us still pay. If nothing gets agreed by 2030, ten years will have been wasted and the rewards will go to a few.

say: I'd say this is the best case and we should build **retraining** and a shorter week.
I'd say people should push now, while there's time.
think: By 34 I could have a **career** and a flat.
I worry the **gains** go to owners, not people like my mum.
do: Get a first job and aim for **client-facing** work.
Pay the loan down steadily and save a deposit.
Teach others the AI tools I learn.
feel: **Calmer**, an almost normal worry about rent and loans.
S4.quote: If nothing gets agreed by 2030, ten years will have been wasted and the rewards will go to a few.
fieldNote: Decade-long time lowers fear but not the **debt** pressure.
Wants to become a **teacher** of tools, playing to his steady, helpful style.
Still thinks in terms of who gets the **gains**.

steps.text: Aim for client-facing analytics roles after graduating
Save a flat deposit while paying the loan
Back groups pushing for training funds before 2030

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2-year one, no question. I'd have no time and a delivery bike. What would help is a real income floor, paid retraining, and a rule that firms must hire and train graduates.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what I enjoy. I love explaining a messy set of sales numbers so a shop owner suddenly gets it. That's why I picked analytics.

headlineQuote: I love explaining a messy set of sales numbers so a shop owner suddenly gets it.
portrait: Emeka is a **24-year-old** master's student in marketing analytics in Manchester, with heavy debt and no internship.
He is **progressive**: blames employers and government, joins the riders' group and wants income floors and training funds.
He is **steady** with AI, using a chatbot for data and drafts and learning tools once they are proven.
His mood runs **anxious** except in the 2-year world, where he is alarmed and moves back to his parents.
Delivery shifts on an e-bike and his parents' **taxi and care-home** work shape his fallback plans.
biggestWorry: Emeka fears **2028** most, with no time and a delivery bike for a job.
whatWouldHelp: He wants a **basic income floor**, paid retraining and rules forcing firms to train graduates.
